Embedding external functions in GGIR

Source: vignettes/ExternalFunction.Rmd
ExternalFunction.Rmd

NOTE: If you are viewing this page via CRAN note that the main GGIR documentation has been migrated to the GGIR GitHub pages.

Introduction

If you like GGIR but want to use algorithms for raw data not included in GGIR then the external function embedding feature can be the solution. For example, you may want to pilot a new machine learned classifiction algorithm but you do not want to write all the data cleaning and aggregation steps needed for analysis of real life ‘out of the lab’ acceleormeter data.

How it works:

Internally GGIR loads the raw accelerometer data in memory blocks of about 24 hours. When the data is in memory, corrected for calibration error, and resampled to the sample rate required by your function, GGIR applies its own default algorithms as well as the external function provided by you (Python or R). The external function is expected to take as input: A three-column matrix with the acceleration data corresponding to the three acceleration axes, and an optional parameters argument which can be of any R format (character, list, vector, data.frame, etc). As output your external function is expected to produce a matrix or data.frame with one or multiple columns corresponding to the output of your external function.

Example with external R function

In this example we will apply the function counts() from R package activityCounts to the raw data, which produces an estimate of Actigraph counts per second.

Write external function

Create file calculateCounts.R and insert the following code:

calculateCounts = function(data=c(), parameters=c()) {
  # data: 3 column matrix with acc data
  # parameters: the sample rate of data
  library("activityCounts")
  if (ncol(data) == 4) data = data[,2:4]
  mycounts = counts(data = data, hertz = parameters, 
                    x_axis = 1, y_axis = 2, z_axis = 3,
                    start_time = Sys.time())
  mycounts = mycounts[,2:4] #Note: do not provide timestamps to GGIR
  return(mycounts)
}

Provide external function to GGIR

Create a new .R file for running the GGIR analysis, e.g. named myscript.R, and insert the following code. Do not forget to update the filepath on the first line to point to your calculateCounts.R file.

source("~/calculateCounts.R")
myfun =  list(FUN = calculateCounts,
              parameters = 30,
              expected_sample_rate = 30,
              expected_unit = "g",
              colnames = c("countsX","countsY","countsZ"),
              outputres = 1,
              minlength = 1,
              outputtype = "numeric",
              aggfunction = sum,
              timestamp = F,
              reporttype = c("scalar", "scalar", "scalar"))

The above code creates object myfun of type list which is expected to come with the following elements:

  • FUN A character string specifying the location of the external function you want to apply.
  • parameters The parameters used by the function, which can be stored in any format (vector, matrix, list, data.frame). The user should make sure that the external function can handle this object.
  • expected_sample_rate Expected sample rate, if the inputdata has a difference sample rate, then the data will be resampled.
  • expected_unit Expected unit of the acceleration by external function: “mg”, “g” or “ms2”. If input data is different it will be converted.
  • colnames Character vector with the names of the columns produced by the external function.
  • outputres The resolution (seconds) of the output produced by the external function. Note, that this needs to be equal to or a multitude of the short epoch size of the g.part1 output (5 seconds) or the short epoch size should be a multitude of this resolution. In this way GGIR can aggregate or repeat the external function output to be used inside GGIR, see Aggregation and missing values.
  • minlength The minimum length (seconds) of input data needed, typically the window per which output is provided.
  • outputtype Character to indicate the type of external function output. Set to “numeric” if data is stored in numbers (any numeric format), or “character” if it is a character string. Provide either one value for all output columns or one value per column, e.g. c("numeric", "character").
  • aggfunction If the data needs to be aggregated to match the short epoch size of the g.part1 output (5 seconds) then this element specifies what function should be used for the aggregation, e.g. mean, sum, median. Provide either one function for all output columns or a list with one function per column. See Aggregation and missing values for when it is required and how missing values are handled.
  • timestamp Boolean to indicate whether timestamps (seconds since 1-1-1970) should be passed to the external function as the first column of the data matrix. The external function may then return either only its output columns, or the timestamp as an additional first column.
  • reporttype Character to indicate the type of reporting by GGIR: “scalar” if it should be averaged per day, “event” if it should be summed per day, or “type” if it is a categorical variable that should be tabulated (see External functions with categorical output for an example). Provide either one value for all output columns or one value per column. For backward compatibility, GGIR treats outputs as "scalar" when reporttype is omitted. For reporttype = "event", GGIR stores the summaries in part2_eventsummary.csv and part2_dayeventsummary.csv rather than part2_summary.csv and part2_daysummary.csv. When several event columns are returned, their column names are included in event summary variable names to keep the results distinct.
  • name Character to indicate the name of the entity being detected in the cases of event detection, this name is used in the output filename, e.g. part2_stepsummary.csv when name is “step”. At the moment name is only use for event detection algorithms

Next, add a call to GGIR function GGIR with myfun provided as one of its arguments:

library(GGIR)
GGIR(datadir = "~/myaccelerometerdata",
             outputdir = "~/myresults",
             mode = 1:2,
             epochvalues2csv = TRUE,
             do.report = 2,
             myfun = myfun) #<= this is where object myfun is provided to GGIR

Please see the for more information about function GGIR.

Example with external Python function

In this example we will use an external Python function to estimate the dominant signal frequency per acceleration axis. Note this can also be done in R, but it shows that even Python functions can be provided.

Write external function

Create dominant_frequency.py and insert the code shown below:

import numpy

def dominant_frequency(x, sf):
  # x: vector with data values
  # sf: sample frequency
  fourier = numpy.fft.fft(x)
  frequencies = numpy.fft.fftfreq(len(x), 1/sf)
  magnitudes = abs(fourier[numpy.where(frequencies > 0)])
  peak_frequency = frequencies[numpy.argmax(magnitudes)]
  return peak_frequency

Create dominant_frequency.R that calls the python function and insert the following code:

dominant_frequency = function(data=c(), parameters=c()) {
  # data: 3 column matrix with acc data
  # parameters: the sample rate of data
  source_python("dominant_frequency.py")
  sf=parameters
  N = nrow(data)
  ws = 5 # windowsize
  if (ncol(data) == 4) data= data[,2:4]
  data = data.frame(t = floor(seq(0,(N - 1)/sf, by = 1/sf)/ws),
                    x = data[,1], y = data[,2], z = data[,3])
  df = aggregate(data, by = list(data$t), 
                 FUN=function(x) {return(dominant_frequency(x, sf))})
  df = df[, -c(1:2)]
  return(df)
}
}

Provide external function to GGIR

Create a new .R file for running the GGIR analysis, e.g. named myscript.R, and insert the following blocks of code.

Specification of Python environment to use, this can also be a conda environment or docker container (see documentation R package for further details). Make sure that that this Python environment has all the required dependencies for the external function, here we will only need numpy.

  library("reticulate")
  use_virtualenv("~/myvenv", required = TRUE) # Local Python environment
  py_install("numpy", pip = TRUE)

Specify a myfun object as explained in the R example. Do not forget to update the filepath to the "~/dominant_frequency.R" file.

source("~/dominant_frequency.R")
myfun =  list(FUN = dominant_frequency,
              parameters = 30,
              expected_sample_rate = 30,
              expected_unit = "g",
              colnames = c("domfreqX", "domfreqY", "domfreqZ"),
              minlength = 5,
              outputres = 5,
              outputtype = "numeric",
              aggfunction = median
              timestamp = F,
              reporttype = c("scalar", "scalar", "scalar"))

Add a call to function GGIR where myfun is provided as argument. Note that, do.parallel is set to FALSE. Unfortunately Python embedding with R package reticulate and multi-threading with R package foreach as used in GGIR do not combine well.

library(GGIR)
GGIR(datadir = "~/myaccelerometerdata",
             outputdir = "~/myresults",
             mode = 1:2,
             epochvalues2csv = TRUE,
             do.report = 2,
             myfun = myfun,
             do.parallel = FALSE)

Multiple output columns

An external function can return more than one output column, for example as a data.frame or a matrix. Each column is described by the corresponding value in colnames, which must be unique. Elements outputtype, reporttype and aggfunction can be given either as a single value that applies to all columns, or as one value per column in the same order as colnames. This makes it possible to combine different kinds of output in one function, for example a categorical activity type together with a numeric intensity:

myfun$colnames = c("activity", "intensity")
myfun$outputtype = c("character", "numeric")
myfun$reporttype = c("type", "scalar")
myfun$aggfunction = list(function(x) x[1], mean)

Each output column is processed and reported independently according to its own outputtype and reporttype.

Aggregation and missing values

When outputres is shorter than the short epoch size of GGIR (first value of argument windowsizes), GGIR aggregates the values of each epoch with aggfunction, and aggfunction must be provided. When outputres equals the epoch size the output is used as is, and when outputres is longer GGIR repeats each value to fill the epochs it covers; in both cases aggfunction is not needed.

When the output columns need different aggregation, for example when numeric and character outputs are combined, provide aggfunction as a list with one function per output column.

GGIR passes all values of each epoch to aggfunction, including missing values (NA) produced by the external function. Epochs containing only missing values are retained, preserving time alignment; their aggregated value depends on aggfunction. For example, function(x) sum(x, na.rm = TRUE) returns 0 for an all-missing epoch. Missing values are handled as follows:

  • mean, sum and similar functions return NA if any value in the epoch is missing. Use function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) to summarise the available values instead.
  • function(x) x[1] returns NA when the first value is missing, even if later values in the epoch are not missing.
  • For character outputs, a function that selects the most frequent value should convert to character before tabulating and return NA when all values are missing:
function(x) {
  counts = table(as.character(x))
  if (length(counts) == 0) NA_character_ else names(which.max(counts))
}

Character outputs reach aggfunction as factors, and table() on a factor also counts levels that do not occur, so a plain names(sort(table(x), decreasing = TRUE))[1] would assign the first level to epochs in which all values are missing.

Integration in GGIR output

Part 1

The external function output is included in the time series produced by function GGIR function g.part1 and stored in an RData-file in /output_nameofstudy/meta/basic. The resolution of these output in GGIR is set by GGIR argument windowsizes, which is c(5,900,3600) by default. Here, the first element 5 specifies the short epoch size in seconds. If the output of the external function is less then this resolution it will be aggregated with the function as specificied by aggfunction in the myfun object (see Aggregation and missing values). In the count example we used the sum for this and for the dominant frequency example we used the median.

Part 2

Next, in part2 GGIR aims to detect non-wear periods and imputes those. The impute time series can be found in the part 2 milestone data in folder: /output_nameofstudy/meta/ms2.out. If you want these to be directly stored in a csv file then set argument epochvalues2csv = TRUE.

Part 5

Part 5 summarises the time series per day, separately for the sustained sleep period (spt) and the time outside the sustained sleep period (day). At the moment only outputs with reporttype = "type" are summarised in part 5. GGIR writes them to dedicated reports per output column, named part5_extfuntype_<column>_daysummary_<window>_<sleep-definition>.csv and part5_extfuntype_<column>_personsummary_<window>_<sleep-definition>.csv. These contain the time, mean acceleration, and number of blocks and bouts per category, separately for spt and day. See External functions with categorical output for a description of these variables.

Outputs with reporttype = "scalar" or "event" are not summarised in part 5. The only exception is an event output named step_count, which part 5 keeps in its time series (folder /output_nameofstudy/meta/ms5.outraw, saved by default via save_ms5rawlevels = TRUE) and in the visual report, but not in the part 5 summary reports.

Visual report

When visualreport = TRUE, the visual report that GGIR generates after part 5 also shows external function output:

  • reporttype = "type": the output column is drawn as a coloured strip below the main plot, with one colour per category and the categories listed in the legend. When the time series is aggregated to a longer epoch (for example with part5_agg2_60seconds = TRUE), each epoch shows the category that took up most of its time. Epochs without a category (unclassified or invalid) are left blank.
  • reporttype = "event": the output column is drawn as vertical bars at the bottom of the plot, showing the number of events per minute. The bars are scaled to 120 per minute for an output named step_count, and to the highest rate in the recording otherwise. Note that part 5 currently only keeps an event output named step_count in its time series, so event outputs with other names are not shown.
  • reporttype = "scalar": these outputs are not shown in the visual report.

If several output columns have the same reporttype, only the first of them (in the order of colnames) is plotted. All output columns are still included in the CSV reports.

External functions released by GGIR collaborators:

  • Wrist-based step detection algorithm: https://github.com/ShimmerResearch/Verisense-Toolbox/tree/master/Verisense_step_algorithm

which is not actively maintained, for the latest version of the function see: https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/master/user-scripts/verisense_count_steps.R

  • Wrist-based sleep classification as described by Sundararajan et al. 2021 link to paper, and corresponding code is here: https://github.com/wadpac/Sundararajan-SleepClassification-2021/tree/master/ggir_ext
